topics.title: Reflection of Light and Image Formation by Plane and Spherical Mirrors

concepts.label: Laws of Reflection and the Image in a Plane Mirror
concepts.cardText: An object reflects light that falls on it, and when this reflected light is received by our eyes we see the object. A highly polished surface, such as a mirror, reflects most of the light falling on it. The laws of reflection are: the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. These laws apply to all types of reflecting surfaces, including spherical surfaces. The image formed by a plane mirror is always virtual and erect, the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, and laterally inverted.

concepts.label: Spherical Mirrors: Concave and Convex, and Their Terms
concepts.cardText: Mirrors whose reflecting surfaces are spherical are called spherical mirrors. If the reflecting surface is curved inwards, facing the centre of the sphere, it is a concave mirror; if curved outwards, a convex mirror. The centre of the reflecting surface is the pole P. The reflecting surface forms part of a sphere whose centre, C, is the centre of curvature; it is not part of the mirror, lies in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex mirror. The radius of that sphere is the radius of curvature R, equal to PC. The straight line through the pole and the centre of curvature is the principal axis, normal to the mirror at its pole.

concepts.label: Principal Focus, Focal Length and R = 2f
concepts.cardText: Sunlight directed by a concave mirror onto paper converges to a sharp, bright spot, the focus, and the heat can ignite the paper. Rays parallel to the principal axis, after reflection from a concave mirror, meet at a point on the axis called the principal focus. For a convex mirror the reflected rays appear to come from a point on the axis, the principal focus. The principal focus is F, and the distance between the pole and the principal focus is the focal length f. The diameter of the reflecting surface is its aperture. For spherical mirrors of small aperture, the radius of curvature is twice the focal length, R = 2f, so the principal focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature.

concepts.label: Image Formation by a Concave Mirror
concepts.cardText: The nature, position and size of the image formed by a concave mirror depend on the position of the object in relation to the points P, F and C. The image is real for some positions and virtual for one other. It is magnified, reduced or the same size depending on the position. A real, inverted image forms when the object is beyond C (diminished, between F and C), at C (same size, at C), or between C and F (enlarged, beyond C). At infinity the image is highly diminished and point-sized at F. When the object is at F, the image is at infinity. Only when the object is between P and F is the image virtual, erect, enlarged and behind the mirror. Concave mirrors are used in torches, headlights, shaving mirrors, dentists' mirrors and solar furnaces.

concepts.label: Image Formation by a Convex Mirror and Its Uses
concepts.cardText: For a convex mirror two object positions are considered. When the object is at infinity the image is at the focus F behind the mirror, highly diminished and point-sized, virtual and erect. When the object is between infinity and the pole P, the image is between P and F behind the mirror, diminished, virtual and erect. You can see a full-length image of a tall building in a small convex mirror, as in the one fitted in a wall of Agra Fort facing the Taj Mahal. Convex mirrors are used as rear-view (wing) mirrors in vehicles, because they always give an erect though diminished image and, being curved outwards, have a wider field of view, so the driver sees a much larger area than with a plane mirror.

topics.title: Ray Diagrams, Sign Convention, Mirror Formula and Magnification

concepts.label: Ray Diagrams for Spherical Mirrors
concepts.cardText: An extended object acts as many point sources, each sending out an infinite number of rays, but for clarity two rays are chosen whose directions after reflection are easy to know. The intersection of at least two reflected rays gives the position of the image. Any two of four rays can be used: (i) a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the principal focus after reflection in a concave mirror, or appears to diverge from it in a convex mirror; (ii) a ray through the principal focus of a concave mirror, or directed towards that of a convex mirror, emerges parallel to the axis; (iii) a ray through the centre of curvature, or directed towards it, is reflected back along the same path, because it falls along the normal; (iv) a ray incident obliquely at the pole is reflected obliquely at an equal angle. In all cases the laws of reflection are followed.
concepts.hint: Which rays can be used to locate the image formed by a spherical mirror and how does each behave?
concepts.probe: Explain the rays used in ray diagrams for spherical mirrors and how each is reflected.
concepts.causeChain: The image of a point is where at least two reflected rays intersect -> parallel rays go through (or appear from) the principal focus, and rays through the focus come out parallel -> a ray through the centre of curvature returns along its own path, and an oblique ray at the pole is reflected at an equal angle

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the choice of easy rays to the intersection that locates the image.

keyPoints.text: Each small portion of an extended object acts like a point source. To construct ray diagrams it is more convenient to consider only two rays, chosen so that it is easy to know their directions after reflection from the mirror. The intersection of at least two reflected rays gives the position of the image of the point object.

checks.criterion: States that a ray diagram uses two convenient rays whose directions after reflection are known, and the intersection of at least two reflected rays gives the position of the image.

A ray through the centre of curvature is reflected back along the same path because it falls along the normal. A ray incident obliquely at the pole is reflected obliquely at an equal angle.

concepts.label: New Cartesian Sign Convention for Mirrors
concepts.cardText: While dealing with reflection by spherical mirrors we follow the New Cartesian Sign Convention. The pole of the mirror is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis. The object is always placed to the left of the mirror, so light falls on it from the left. All distances parallel to the principal axis are measured from the pole. Distances to the right of the origin (along +x) are positive, while those to the left (along -x) are negative. Distances measured perpendicular to and above the principal axis (along +y) are positive, and those below (along -y) are negative. These sign conventions are applied to obtain the mirror formula and solve numerical problems.

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the origin and axis to the positive and negative directions.

concepts.label: Mirror Formula and Magnification
concepts.cardText: In a spherical mirror the distance of the object from the pole is the object distance u, the distance of the image from the pole is the image distance v, and the distance of the principal focus from the pole is the focal length f. These are related by the mirror formula, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, valid in all situations for all spherical mirrors and all positions of the object, as long as the New Cartesian Sign Convention is used. Magnification m is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, m = h'/h, and is also -v/u. A negative sign for m indicates that the image is real; a positive sign indicates that it is virtual.

concepts.causeChain: Object distance u, image distance v and focal length f are related by the mirror formula, using the sign convention -> magnification is the ratio of image height to object height and equals -v/u -> a negative magnification means a real image and a positive one a virtual image

causeLinks.criterion: Connects u, v and f in the mirror formula to magnification and the meaning of its sign.

keyPoints.text: In a spherical mirror, the distance of the object from its pole is called the object distance (u), the distance of the image from the pole is the image distance (v), and the distance of the principal focus from the pole is the focal length (f). This formula is valid in all situations for all spherical mirrors for all positions of the object, using the New Cartesian Sign Convention.

keyPoints.text: Magnification produced by a spherical mirror gives the relative extent to which the image of an object is magnified with respect to the object size. It is expressed as the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, and is also related to the object distance and image distance. A negative sign in the value of the magnification indicates that the image is real. A positive sign indicates that the image is virtual.

checks.criterion: States that magnification is the ratio of image height to object height (also related to u and v), a negative value means a real image and a positive value a virtual image.

topics.title: Refraction of Light, Snell's Law and Absolute Refractive Index

concepts.label: Refraction of Light: Bending Between Media
concepts.cardText: The bottom of a pond appears raised, letters under a glass slab appear raised, and a pencil partly in water appears displaced at the interface. The light from the part of the pencil inside water seems to come from a different direction compared with the part above it, and the effect differs for different pairs of media. When light travels obliquely from one medium to another, its direction of propagation in the second medium changes: this is refraction. Through a rectangular glass slab the ray bends towards the normal on entering the denser glass and away from the normal on leaving into the rarer air. The bending at the two parallel faces is equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, but shifted sideways. Refraction is due to a change in the speed of light as it enters from one transparent medium to another.

keyPoints.text: Light does not travel in the same direction in all media. When travelling obliquely from one medium to another, the direction of propagation of light in the second medium changes. This phenomenon is known as refraction of light. Refraction is due to change in the speed of light as it enters from one transparent medium to another.

concepts.label: Laws of Refraction and Snell's Law
concepts.cardText: Refraction of light follows two laws. First, the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. Second, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, for light of a given colour and for the given pair of media. This is also known as Snell's law of refraction, true for angles between 0 and 90 degrees. If i is the angle of incidence and r the angle of refraction, sin i / sin r is a constant, and this constant value is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

concepts.label: Refractive Index and Optical Density
concepts.cardText: Light travels fastest in vacuum, at 3×10^8 m/s; in air it is only marginally less, and it reduces considerably in glass or water. The refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is the ratio of the speed of light in medium 1 to its speed in medium 2. If medium 1 is vacuum or air, this is the absolute refractive index of the medium, the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed in the medium. For example water has n = 1.33 and crown glass 1.52. The medium with the larger refractive index is optically denser, which may not mean greater mass density: kerosene is optically denser than water though lighter. Light speeds are higher in a rarer medium, so a ray going rarer to denser slows down and bends towards the normal, and going denser to rarer speeds up and bends away from the normal.

topics.title: Image Formation by Spherical Lenses, Lens Formula and Power of a Lens

concepts.label: Convex and Concave Lenses and Their Terms
concepts.cardText: A transparent material bound by two surfaces, of which one or both are spherical, forms a lens. A double convex lens bulges outwards on both sides, is thicker at the middle than at the edges and converges light rays, so it is a converging lens. A double concave lens is curved inwards, thicker at the edges than at the middle, and diverges light rays, so it is a diverging lens. The centres of the two spheres are the centres of curvature C1 and C2, and the line through them is the principal axis. The central point is the optical centre O, and a ray through it passes without any deviation. The aperture is the effective diameter of the lens outline. Parallel rays converge to the principal focus of a convex lens, or appear to diverge from that of a concave lens; a lens has two principal foci, F1 and F2, and the distance from the optical centre to a focus is the focal length f.

concepts.label: Image Formation by Convex and Concave Lenses
concepts.cardText: Lenses form images by refracting light. For a convex lens the image depends on the object's position relative to F and 2F. A real, inverted image forms when the object is at infinity (at F2, point-sized), beyond 2F1 (between F2 and 2F2, diminished), at 2F1 (at 2F2, same size) or between F1 and 2F1 (beyond 2F2, enlarged). At F1 the image is at infinity. Between F1 and the optical centre the image is virtual, erect and enlarged, on the same side as the object. A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image, irrespective of the position of the object, between the focus F1 and the optical centre. For ray diagrams, any two of three rays are used: a parallel ray through the focus, a ray through the focus emerging parallel, and a ray through the optical centre undeviated.

concepts.label: Lens Formula, Sign Convention and Magnification
concepts.cardText: For lenses we follow a sign convention similar to the one for spherical mirrors, with all distances measured from the optical centre. The focal length of a convex lens is positive and that of a concave lens is negative. The lens formula gives the relationship between the object distance u, image distance v and focal length f, 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. It is general and valid in all situations for any spherical lens, but signs must be applied properly. Magnification by a lens is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, m = h'/h, which is also v/u. A positive magnification means an erect, virtual image and a negative one an inverted, real image.

concepts.label: Power of a Lens and the Dioptre
concepts.cardText: The ability of a lens to converge or diverge light rays depends on its focal length: a convex lens of short focal length bends rays through large angles, and a concave lens of very short focal length causes higher divergence. This degree of convergence or divergence is expressed as the power of the lens, the reciprocal of its focal length: P = 1/f. The SI unit of power is the dioptre, D; if f is in metres, power is in dioptres, so 1 dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length 1 metre. The power of a convex lens is positive and of a concave lens negative. A prescription of +2.0 D means a convex lens of focal length +0.50 m, and -2.5 D a concave lens of focal length -0.40 m. The net power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum of their individual powers.
